_about: Lines in the region that are not railways. The Skaguay works are written by atlas/tools/once_skaguay_pipeline.py and the Old Stage Road by once_old_stage_road.py; drawn by web/region.html. Not checked by validate.py.

properties.name: Skaguay pipeline, from the dam to the first side valley
properties.basis: A thin continuous line on fine-relief pictures of the 1 m lidar, from the gorge below the dam's spillway, round the spur and south along the west side of the valley, through the place where the owner photographed the wood-stave pipe. The ground on it reads 8,847 to 8,856 ft at nearly every point for over a mile. Hardesty's account of 1903 says the pipe was laid on a grade of 1 in 2,000 from a head at 9,018 ft by the company's levels, which are about 168 ft above the lidar's (spillway 9,081 against 8,912.5): so the pipe should stand at about 8,850 ft here, and it does. Taken to be the pipe's bed, with a later trail on it.

properties.name: Skaguay pipeline, on its grade to the tunnel (drawn from the 1903 figures; not seen on the ground)
properties.basis: Not seen. This is the level the pipe must have kept by the published figures (a fall of 1 in 2,000: about 8,846 ft here, 8,839 ft at the tunnel), followed along the west side of the canyon, which is the side Hardesty names. No bench or line shows on the lidar at this level, even on smooth slopes where the trail 50 ft below shows plainly; the pipe was taken up after 1965 and seems to have left little mark. How it crossed the side valleys is not known. By this line the tunnel's north end comes at about 20,200 to 21,600 ft from the dam, against 20,000 to 21,000 in the sources.

properties.name: The Skaguay tunnel (placed from the 1903 figures and a 1902 photograph; portals not seen)
properties.basis: Hardesty, 1903: 'nearly vertical cliffs form a bold projection... Through this projection the Skaguay tunnel is run. This is 1,536 ft. long', its north heading turning 'about 23 degrees to the right'; a standpipe stood 'just outside the lower end of the tunnel', and the inclined railway's upper end was there too. Drawn to fit: the south end under the terrace at 8,916 ft where the incline tops out; the north end at the foot of the projection's cliffs on the south wall of the side valley, at the pipe's level (8,840 ft); two legs of about 760 ft, the second turned 23 degrees to the right as one goes in from the north, 1,521 ft in all. The north end is put there, and not at a hollow about 480 ft further west that also fits the length, for two reasons, neither strong: the skyline in a photograph of 1902 captioned 'Wood Stave Pipe, Showing North End of Skaguay Tunnel' matches the lidar best from a camera at the head of the side valley looking south-east toward those cliffs (a moderate fit at best: the print is coarse and the lens unknown); and with the western point the published turn would be to the left. No portal, and no bench for the pipe, shows on the lidar at either place, though the photograph shows the pipe on a cut bench. A fit to the sources, not a finding.

properties.name: Inclined railway to the Skaguay power plant, lower part
properties.basis: A dead-straight cut up the slope from the plant's pad, plain on the 1 m lidar and drawn on the 1951 USGS map. The engineering press of 1902-1907 describes an inclined railway from the tunnel's lower end to the power house, rising 1,165 ft in 3,100 ft, with the steel pressure pipe beside it; its steepest part, 56.6 per cent, is this lower stretch (56 per cent on the lidar).

properties.name: Inclined railway to the Skaguay power plant, upper part (through its tunnel)
properties.basis: Above the straight cut the line is rough, then meets a cliff where the ground jumps 260 ft in 170 ft: too steep for open track, and taken to be the inclined tunnel the sources give as 335 or 363 ft long, whose exact line is not found. It comes out on the plateau and ends at a terrace at 8,916 ft. Measured along this course the incline is about 3,130 ft on the level and rises 1,168 ft, against 3,100 and 1,165 in the sources.

properties.name: Trail from the dam to the power plant, across the side valley
properties.basis: A line plain on the lidar that leaves the pipe's bed, falls at about 10 per cent to the floor of a side valley and climbs out again. First taken for the pipe; it is 100 ft below the pipe's published grade here. The Electrical Review of January 1907 says a horse trail from the dam to the power house 'had just been completed': taken to be that trail.

properties.name: Trail from the dam to the power plant, along the canyon side
properties.basis: A thin line plain on the lidar, holding 8,785 to 8,803 ft for over a mile and dropping straight through the gullies it meets. First taken for the pipe; it runs about 50 ft below the pipe's published grade, and by it the tunnel would come 2,000 ft too soon. Taken to be the horse trail of 1907; it goes on by a track to the top of the incline.

properties.name: Old Stage Road, the lower end from the Broadmoor side
properties.basis: Today's paved road from its lower end up the ravine to the hairpin where the pavement ends, from OpenStreetMap; it lies on the road surface on the 1 m lidar. That the stage road came up this way is inferred from two government sheets. The sheet of 1893 (1:125,000) draws the road coming from the north-east, from the Cheyenne Creek side, running south and then turning west up the mountain; it does not touch South Cheyenne Creek. The sheet of 1909 draws a road of the same shape from Broadmoor, and today's road lies on it. The 1893 sheet is displaced about 900 ft against the ground all along this road, so it gives the road's course and not its place; the place is today's road, good to perhaps 300 ft as the line of the 1890s. The 1909 sheet also draws a lesser road north from the hairpin to the South Cheyenne Canon road; that one is not on the 1893 sheet. No abandoned bench was seen beside today's road.

properties.name: Old Stage Road: the Cheyenne Mountain road to Cripple Creek, over the mountain to the Short Line
properties.basis: Today's unpaved Old Stage Road from the hairpin where the pavement ends, over the shoulder of Cheyenne Mountain past Wade's, down to Rock Creek and up to Gold Camp Road, from OpenStreetMap; it lies on the road surface on the 1 m lidar throughout. That this is the line of the stage road is inferred: the government sheet of 1909 (1:125,000, surveyed 1906-07) draws its road within about 50 ft of today's at the middle point and within 200 ft at nearly every point, which is as close as that sheet puts the railway here, and the lidar shows no abandoned bench beside it. The government sheet of 1893 (1:125,000), read since, draws a road of the same course over the mountain, before any railway; it is displaced about 900 ft against the ground the same way all along, so it confirms the course and places nothing. About 6.6 miles, climbing from about 6,900 ft to 9,034 ft; one true switchback, at the bottom; no bridge and no large fill. At Rock Creek the road passes through the gap of the Short Line's trestle, about 44 ft below the track, and it meets the railway's grade on the level just west of Tunnel No. 7. The road is older than the Cripple Creek rush: newspapers (machine text, not checked on the page) have a Cheyenne Mountain toll road as a pleasure drive in 1876, to East Beaver Creek by 1878 and to Seven Lakes in 1881. In January 1892 a committee of the Colorado Springs Chamber of Commerce recommended extending it to Cripple Creek as the cheapest route, free of toll; a later account says the county built the extension in four months. Coaches were running by April 1893 and still in 1899; the road fell out of use after the Short Line opened in 1901, was called the old stage road by 1905, and was mended for motor cars from about 1912. No record of its opening day has been found. It is shown here from 1892, the year of the extension; how far the road of the 1870s ran on this same line is not known.

properties.name: Cripple Creek stage road beyond the Short Line, as mapped in 1909 (today's Gold Camp Road and Bear Trap Road)
properties.basis: Beyond the meeting with the railway the government sheet of 1909 draws the road north-west to a hairpin with two buildings, then down into the valley of Rock Creek. Today's Gold Camp Road and Bear Trap Road (Forest Road 370.A) lie on that line to about 150 ft, and are drawn here from OpenStreetMap. This is the road as it stood after the railway was built; where it ran through the ground of the railway's loop before 1900 is not known.

properties.name: Abandoned road bench from Bear Trap Road to the Short Line's fill at Summit (taken to be the stage road)
properties.basis: A bench the width of a road along the north edge of the valley floor, read by eye from the 1 m and 0.5 m lidar; it is on no modern map. It climbs at about 9 per cent for 4,200 ft and stops at the foot of the Short Line's embankment at the Summit loop, which stands 55 to 60 ft above it with no opening seen. The bench itself is measured, to about 40 ft. That it is the stage road is inferred: it lies where the sheet of 1909 draws the road west to Summit, within about 550 ft of the drawn line, and the railway's fill of 1900-01 lies across its end. The road is found again at the fill's west foot, on the same line and grade (see the next piece). The government sheet of 1893 draws the road running on west up this valley toward Rosemont with no railway on the map, which supports the bench being that road; the sheet is too coarse and too displaced to prove it.

properties.name: Cripple Creek stage road: abandoned road across the Summit loop and along the valley floor
properties.basis: West of the railway's fill the road is found again. At the fill's west foot, opposite the buried end of the bench and on the same grade, a faint straight line cut a foot or so into the slope climbs at 11 to 12 per cent across the inside of the Short Line's loop, and beyond the loop it becomes a plain abandoned road on the valley floor for 0.3 mile; all read from the 1 m lidar, and on no modern map. The government sheet of 1909 draws its road within about 65 ft of the valley road. That this is the stage road is inferred from its line and grade matching the bench and from that sheet. The 60 ft under the fill is drawn straight across. Whether the road crossed the loop's west arm at grade is not settled. The government sheet of 1948 (Mount Big Chief, 1:24,000) draws a road up Little Fountain Creek and across the floor of the loop to the saddle on this line: a second map for it, though a late one.

properties.name: Cripple Creek stage road: past Summit station to the south end of Rosemont Reservoir
properties.basis: On the government sheet of 1909 the road runs past Summit station, where today's Gold Camp Road on the railway's grade lies 30 to 200 ft from it, and then south-west across the open slope to where the reservoir's south end now is. On the 1 m lidar only faint narrow ruts run that way; there is no bench. The sheet of 1893 draws a different road here, north-west toward Rosemont station and along the north slope; that one was not found on the ground and is not drawn (research/old-stage-road/route-west-alternatives.geojson). The sheet of 1948 has no road on this line, nor on the 1893 sheet's north-slope course; a close search of the lidar found neither. Not settled.

properties.name: Cripple Creek stage road: under Rosemont Reservoir (placed from the 1909 map alone)
properties.basis: The road of the 1909 sheet from the reservoir's south end west across its southern arm, 0.6 mile now under water, and on to Forest Road 372. Nothing can be seen; placed by that 1:125,000 sheet alone. East Beaver Park, which the reservoir fills, is the widest flat ground on the whole road.

properties.name: Cripple Creek stage road: down East Beaver Creek (Forest Road 372 and Gold Camp Road)
properties.basis: Forest Road 372 and a track on the valley floor below the reservoir, then Gold Camp Road on the Short Line's grade down East Beaver valley to where the railway turns south into its loops. The government sheet of 1909 draws its road within 15 to 200 ft of these. Whether the stage road lay under the railway's bed or beside it on the valley floor is not settled.

properties.name: Cripple Creek stage road: Gold Camp Road to the railway's hairpin above the loops
properties.basis: Gold Camp Road on the Short Line's grade west to the hairpin at the head of the creek that runs south through the railway's loops. The government sheet of 1909 brings its road this far beside the railway. Where the stage road left East Beaver valley is not settled: it may instead have come along the tracks south of the railway, which were not followed.

properties.name: Cripple Creek stage road: from the hairpin down to the head of the abandoned road (not found on the ground)
properties.basis: A short join, 400 ft, dropping about 90 ft from the railway's hairpin to the head of the abandoned road below. No bench was picked out: the railway's cuts and the hairpin take up the ground. Drawn to keep the road whole.

properties.name: Cripple Creek stage road: the abandoned road through the ground of the railway's loops, marked 'Old Stage Road' on the 1951 map, and Clyde Road
properties.basis: The government sheet of 1951 (Big Bull Mountain, 1:24,000) letters OLD STAGE ROAD along a dashed trail in the broad valley south of Clyde, drawn apart from Gold Camp Road; it leaves Clyde Road about half way down, runs east up the valley and north-east into the valley enclosed by the Short Line's loops, and stops at the lower loop. Read on the sheet. On the 1 m lidar an abandoned narrow road lies within 30 to 160 ft of that trail: about a mile down the creek inside the loops (falling 5 to 10 per cent) and along the north side of the valley (about 3 per cent), with a fainter line for the last half mile to Clyde Road. From there the piece follows Clyde Road down to Middle Beaver Creek, where the sheet of 1901 also brings its road. That the abandoned road is the stage road rests on the 1951 lettering, which is a map-maker's name sixty years after the fact, and on the road's wagon grade. Where it meets the railway's lower loop the test of age did not decide: on the south side it ends at the foot of the fill, on the north it runs up onto the bank. This replaces a line drawn from the 1894 sheet alone, which lay 500 to 800 ft south on the hillside and climbed and fell 360 ft more. Clyde itself lies half a mile north of this road up Clyde Road; no road from East Beaver valley over the ridge to Clyde was found.

properties.name: Cripple Creek stage road: from the foot of Clyde Road toward Love (wrong as drawn; from the 1894 map)
properties.basis: Kept from the government sheet of 1894 for want of better, and wrong as drawn: in 0.29 mile it climbs about 380 ft from the foot of Clyde Road to join the next piece on the railway's grade, which no wagon road did. The road more likely kept to the floor of Middle Beaver valley; the 1951 sheet letters a telephone line there, and the telephone line of 1893 followed the road. Not traced.

properties.name: Cripple Creek stage road: up the side valley to Love and on up West Beaver Creek
properties.basis: Gold Camp Road on the Short Line's grade up the side valley to Love, then Beaver Valley Road through Love, where Middle and West Beaver creeks join, and up West Beaver Creek. The government sheet of 1894, made before the railway, draws its road 10 to 550 ft from these roads all the way. The report of January 1892 (read on the page) says the road was to run 'directly through Love's ranch'.

properties.name: Cripple Creek stage road: the floor of West Beaver Creek canyon (from the 1894 map alone)
properties.basis: Where today's Beaver Valley Road climbs away to the north, the sheet of 1894 keeps its road on the floor of the narrow canyon of West Beaver Creek, 500 to 800 ft from today's road. Map only; no bench was picked out on the lidar. Newspapers of 1896 (machine text) have the coach held up in 'a deep canon' at the foot of the long hill below Grassy; this is the only such canyon on the road.

properties.name: Cripple Creek stage road: up West Beaver and Grassy creeks to Grassy (Cameron)
properties.basis: Beaver Valley Road and County Road 81 up West Beaver Creek and Grassy Creek to Grassy. The sheets of 1894 and 1895 draw their road within 460 ft of these roads. The 1894 sheet's 'Gassy Gulch' is this Grassy Creek, so the road said to go up Gassy Gulch and the road said to come up Beaver Creek past Grassy are one road. It crosses the Midland Terminal and the Short Line several times below Grassy.

properties.name: Cripple Creek stage road: Grassy to the head of Bennett Avenue (from the 1895 map alone)
properties.basis: Inside the mining district: from Grassy up the flat, over the saddle south-east of Globe Hill and down to the east end of Bennett Avenue, drawn from the 1:25,000 Cripple Creek special map (surveyed 1894, issued 1895) alone. The ground is mined, dumped on and built over, and nothing of the road was looked for on it.

properties.name: Cripple Creek stage road: down Bennett Avenue, Cripple Creek
properties.basis: Bennett Avenue to a point between Second and Third Streets, taken here as the end of the road. Newspapers of 1896 (machine text) have the coaches coming into town down Bennett Avenue; where the stage office stood in Cripple Creek has not been found, so the end point is a convention, not a known place. By the line drawn in this atlas the whole road is 30.4 to 31.2 miles from Colorado Springs to Cripple Creek, against 26 miles in the estimate of January 1892 and 28 in a later account, so some of the line is too long; a close search of the middle stretch took off only a fifth of a mile, so the excess lies elsewhere: in the road out of Colorado Springs, which is not traced, the lower road, or the district end. See research/old-stage-road/route-middle.md.

properties.name: Mount Manitou incline (the Manitou Incline)
properties.basis: A cable incline, straight from beside the cog road's depot to the shoulder of Mount Manitou. The line is fitted to its cut on the 1 m lidar, on which today's trail of steps lies (the cut holds to the line within about 3 ft): 4,467 ft on the level, 4,941 ft along the slope, rising 1,953 ft from 6,611 to 8,564 ft, 43.7 per cent on average; the steepest 300 ft of today's ground is 69 per cent. The government sheet of 1948 letters it 'Incline Railway'. By a newspaper of November 1907 (machine text, not checked on the page) the Manitou Incline Railway Company bought 'the cable tram road' from Manitou to the summit of Mount Manitou from the Hydro Electric Company and rebuilt it for passengers; the first passenger car ran on 28 June 1908 (machine text). The Gazette of 9 July 1908, read on the page, gives grades of 14 to 68 per cent and says it was 'constructed without any trestle-work whatever'. On the lidar the ground on the line dips up to 27 ft into a gully near the foot, which a cable line must have crossed on an even grade: by that account it was on fill, not a trestle, and none is entered. When the Hydro Electric Company built the first tram, and where the power house stood, were not found. It is shown to 1990, the year later accounts give for its closing; no record of the closing has been read for this atlas.

properties.name: Red Mountain incline (Red Mountain Scenic Railway; later the Red Peak Incline)
properties.basis: A cable incline, not a cog railway: the prospectus in the Gazette of 26 May 1911, read on the page, promises a double track worked by electricity with cables, 3,200 ft from Ruxton Avenue to the summit, with a pavilion on top; no source calls it a rack road. Found on the ground: on the 1 m lidar one dead-straight line runs through seven separate cuts, 3 to 14 ft deep, from the level of Ruxton Avenue to the crest of Red Mountain, the cuts holding to the line within 2 ft, and the government sheet of 1948 draws a railway lettered '(Abandoned)' on the same line within about 15 ft. It is 2,729 ft on the level and rises 914 ft, from 6,404 to 7,318 ft: about 48 and 28 per cent at the bottom, a nearly level 400 ft in the middle, and about 49 per cent up the last pitch, twice the cog road's steepest. Why the middle is level is not known; it may have been a passing place. It crossed over the Colorado Midland near its foot and a hollow below the upper pitch (see the two pins). Newspapers (machine text, not checked on the page): built by Richard Clough and Son from January 1912, advertised as running in July 1912, in receivership in 1913, sold by the sheriff in 1917, run again as the 'Red Peak Incline' in 1922, and sold by the sheriff on 21 July 1925 having 'not been operated for several years'. Its opening day was not found. Shown from 1912 to 1922, the last year it is known to have run.

properties.name: Pikes Peak carriage road: from Prairie Street up the hillside above Cascade
properties.basis: A lane today, climbing north along the hillside west of the village at about 8 per cent and running on into the abandoned bench above it; followed on the 1 m lidar. The newspapers of 1888 and 1889 (machine text) start the road on Prairie Avenue near the hotel, a quarter mile from the depot, and say the first mile 'coils around above Cascade'. That this lane is that first mile is inferred from those words and from the bench it joins; the lane has been rebuilt for houses and is not the old surface.

properties.name: Pikes Peak carriage road: the old switchback above Cascade, left by the highway of 1915
properties.basis: An abandoned bench 10 to 13 ft wide, climbing north-west at 8 to 9 per cent to meet the highway at 38.9062, -104.9826; followed on the 1 m lidar and looked at there by me. The government sheet of 1909 draws the road's hairpin at this place. The Engineering Record of 23 October 1915 (read on the page) says the highway's first two miles 'deviate from the carriage road, adding 1246 ft. to eliminate three bad uncompensated curves', and today's highway does swing wide here to a higher hairpin. A bench cannot be dated from the ground alone: that this is the carriage road of 1888 rests on the 1909 sheet and the engineers' words. The length the highway adds here does not come out at 1,246 ft, the two roads having started at different points.

properties.name: Pikes Peak carriage road: the west arm of the switchback and round into Cascade Creek
properties.basis: The sheet of 1909 draws the road on this line, and the sheet of 1893 the same shape displaced. Drawn on today's highway. The engineers of the automobile highway wrote in 1915 that it 'followed in general' the carriage road but was 'relocated throughout its entire length', so the old road lay near this line and not always on it; no older bench was picked out beside the highway here.

properties.name: Pikes Peak carriage road: up Cascade Creek to the Crystal Creek fork
properties.basis: The government sheet of 1894 draws the road up this valley 150 to 650 ft south of today's highway, which is within that sheet's error; the sheet of 1909 agrees as far as it goes. The newspapers of 1888 (machine text) have the road in upper Cascade Canyon with a nearly level stretch along the creek. Drawn on today's highway. The engineers of the automobile highway wrote in 1915 that it 'followed in general' the carriage road but was 'relocated throughout its entire length', so the old road lay near this line and not always on it; no older bench was picked out beside the highway here.

properties.name: Pikes Peak carriage road: across the Crystal Creek basin, now under the reservoir (from the 1894 map alone)
properties.basis: The sheet of 1894 carries the road straight across the basin where Crystal Creek Reservoir now stands; the highway goes round the water. A line drawn from that sheet alone, good to no better than 600 ft, and not to be seen on the ground.

properties.name: Pikes Peak carriage road: from the reservoir's west arm up to the highway (a bench of unknown age)
properties.basis: A narrow bench climbing about 8 per cent from the reservoir shore to the highway, on the line the 1894 sheet draws; followed on the lidar. It may as well be a road of the reservoir's building as the carriage road: the 1976 revision of the Woodland Park sheet draws an unimproved road here. Kept as the likeliest join.

properties.name: Pikes Peak carriage road: from the reservoir to the Halfway picnic ground
properties.basis: The sheet of 1894 draws the road within about 350 ft of this line. Drawn on today's highway. The engineers of the automobile highway wrote in 1915 that it 'followed in general' the carriage road but was 'relocated throughout its entire length', so the old road lay near this line and not always on it; no older bench was picked out beside the highway here.

properties.name: Pikes Peak carriage road: a cut-off east of the highway at Halfway (may be a trail)
properties.basis: A narrow line, 6 to 10 ft wide, leaves the highway's bend and climbs straight south at 6 to 7 per cent for a third of a mile; the 1894 sheet's road lies within about 260 ft. Faint on the lidar and narrow for a carriage road: it may be a trail. The highway's own curve beside it is the other candidate.

properties.name: Pikes Peak carriage road: from Halfway up to Glen Cove
properties.basis: The sheet of 1894 draws the road within about 400 ft of this line, as one straight run where the highway now has switchbacks. A straight narrow line east of the highway here climbs 12 to 19 per cent, too steep for a road held to 10, and was not used. Drawn on today's highway. The engineers of the automobile highway wrote in 1915 that it 'followed in general' the carriage road but was 'relocated throughout its entire length', so the old road lay near this line and not always on it; no older bench was picked out beside the highway here.

properties.name: Pikes Peak carriage road: Glen Cove, the W switchbacks and the ridge to the summit
properties.basis: The sheets of 1894 and 1951 both draw the road here within about 330 ft of today's highway: the tight zigzags above Glen Cove, the ridge past Devils Playground and the zigzag below the summit, where the 1894 sheet ends it in a small loop. The Engineering Record of 1915 (read on the page) counts ten switchbacks above Glen Cove on the highway, 'six in two W's'; the newspapers of 1888 (machine text) already have the carriage road zigzag in a 'W' with its turns widened to 40 ft. How many of today's hairpins are the carriage road's is not known. Drawn on today's highway. The engineers of the automobile highway wrote in 1915 that it 'followed in general' the carriage road but was 'relocated throughout its entire length', so the old road lay near this line and not always on it; no older bench was picked out beside the highway here.

properties.name: Seven Lakes road: from the stage road at Rosemont to the divide (today's Frosty Park Road)
properties.basis: The carriage branch of the Cheyenne Mountain toll road, opened to Seven Lakes in August 1881 (newspaper, machine text). Drawn on today's Frosty Park Road, 6.2 miles climbing from 9,800 to 11,030 ft at under 4 per cent. The government sheet of 1909 draws a road on this line within 300 to 800 ft; the sheet of 1893 has the same shape, displaced. Whether today's road keeps the bed of 1881 throughout was not tested. No wheeled road reached the summit of Pikes Peak from this side: every map from 1883 to 1909 ends the roads at Seven Lakes and Lake Moraine.

properties.name: Seven Lakes road: the last mile north to the hotel (from old maps; partly under McReynolds Reservoir)
properties.basis: Ellis's map of 1883 and the government sheet of 1893 draw a road here, and the sheet of 1894 a trail; the three agree within about 500 ft. No bench was found on the lidar and the north end is under McReynolds Reservoir. Jackson's photograph of the basin (looked at by me) shows a wagon road with two wheel tracks winding between the lakes to a white building; it could not be matched to this line, the old lake shores being under water.

properties.name: Seven Lakes road from Clyde up Beaver Creek (today's Seven Lakes Road)
properties.basis: Drawn on today's Seven Lakes Road, 3.3 miles from the Short Line at Clyde. The government sheet of 1901 is the first to draw it, within about 330 ft; the sheet of 1894 has no road here. A Short Line booklet of 1908 (read on the page) reaches the lakes from Clyde station 'by trail and carriage road three and a half miles'. About 4,300 ft of today's road is steeper than 12 per cent, so parts of it were rebuilt or were never a carriage road.

properties.name: Seven Lakes road from Clyde: the last stretch to the hotel site
properties.basis: Read off the government sheet of 1951, with which the sheet of 1901 agrees in its pattern of roads. The ground here was reworked for the reservoirs.

properties.name: Seven Lakes to Lake Moraine road: from the hotel site north to Dead Lake
properties.basis: Read off the government sheet of 1951; the sheets of 1894 and 1901 draw the same road. A road shows on the lidar along here but this piece was not fitted to it. The highest ground reached by any road from the south, about 11,000 ft.

properties.name: Seven Lakes to Lake Moraine road: from Dead Lake down the valley to Lake Moraine
properties.basis: A road bench followed on the 1 m lidar for 2.3 miles, falling from 11,010 to 10,200 ft at under 7 per cent; it is on no present-day map. The government sheet of 1894 draws a road within 330 to 650 ft of it, and Ellis's map of 1883 a trail, the 'Seven Lakes & Manitou Trail'. The bench is where the line says, to about 30 ft; that it is the road of 1894, and not a later waterworks road on the same ground, is inferred from the sheet. No wheeled road reached the summit of Pikes Peak from this side: every map from 1883 to 1909 ends the roads at Seven Lakes and Lake Moraine.

properties.name: Lake Moraine to Bear Creek (from the 1909 map alone)
properties.basis: The government sheet of 1909 draws a road from Lake Moraine east and down toward Bear Creek; drawn from that sheet alone, with no bench picked out. The Bear Creek Canon Road Company's wagon road is said to have reached Lake Moraine by 1891-92, replacing the old Bear Creek trail (index entries and machine text). Its lower end toward Colorado Springs is not drawn.

properties.name: Lake Moraine north toward the cog road (from the 1909 map alone)
properties.basis: A road in the lighter symbol on the government sheet of 1909, from Lake Moraine down toward the cog railway in Ruxton Creek. Drawn from that sheet alone; no bench picked out.

properties.name: Seven Lakes Trail to the summit (from the 1883 map; not found on the ground)
properties.basis: Lettered 'Seven Lakes Trail' on Ellis's map: from the hotel up the valley west of the lakes and north-west to the summit, about five miles. A bridle trail for horses and burros, not a road. It is drawn only on Ellis's map of 1883, a railway promoter's map, laid on the ground by a fit good to 500 ft at best; no government sheet draws it and no tread was looked for on the lidar. The line shows roughly where the trail went and nothing more. Guidebooks of 1883 and 1886 (read on the page) say the carriage road ended at the lakes and the peak was reached from there by trail.

properties.name: Seven Lakes and Manitou Trail, past Lake Moraine to Ruxton Creek (from the 1883 map)
properties.basis: Lettered 'Seven Lakes & Manitou Trail' on Ellis's map. A bridle trail for horses and burros, not a road. It is drawn only on Ellis's map of 1883, a railway promoter's map, laid on the ground by a fit good to 500 ft at best; no government sheet draws it and no tread was looked for on the lidar. The line shows roughly where the trail went and nothing more. Between Dead Lake and Lake Moraine it lies within a few hundred feet of the road bench found on the lidar, which is probably this trail made into a road by 1894.

properties.name: Bear Creek Trail, from below the summit toward Colorado Springs (from the 1883 map)
properties.basis: Lettered 'Bear Creek Trail to Col. Springs' on Ellis's map, passing north of Lake Moraine. A bridle trail for horses and burros, not a road. It is drawn only on Ellis's map of 1883, a railway promoter's map, laid on the ground by a fit good to 500 ft at best; no government sheet draws it and no tread was looked for on the lidar. The line shows roughly where the trail went and nothing more. Taken to be the old trail up Bear Creek by Jones Park and the Lake House, in use by the early 1870s: stereoviews of 1870-76 are titled 'from Bear Creek Canon to the summit, 14 miles'. That the Signal Service cut it in 1873 is said only by later books. The fit of the 1883 map is at its worst here.
